## Two sugars, two sugars – and two more volunteers, please

I came to hospice volunteering for a thoroughly ordinary reason: I was at a loose end.

I had retired after 41 years of bookkeeping, mostly for a builders’ merchant in Dereham, and for the next eighteen months I drifted rather. There was no regular reason to go out most weeks. I started on the Thursday tea trolley in the day therapy unit in March 2022, and Thursdays soon put some shape back into my week.

Before I started, I probably had the same worries many people have. I thought a hospice might be unbearably sad, and that everyone working or volunteering there must possess some special skill I did not have.

Most Thursdays, it is not the hushed, sorrowful place people imagine. It is noisy and rather jolly. We usually see between 14 and 18 patients in the day unit. Many come for the art group or the hand massage, or simply for company, and most go home afterwards.

My first week did not begin particularly impressively. I spilled an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much that she had to be given a tissue, and then told me it was the best afternoon she’d had in a month. Nobody suggested I ought to find another occupation, so I stayed.

Since then I have learnt that Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and insists on telling me about the 1953 floods each week. The story is slightly different every time. I have stopped correcting the dates.

I have also learnt that the bourbon biscuits always go first. We now hide a packet for the late group. This is exactly the sort of strategic planning my bookkeeping career prepared me for.

You do not need nursing skills to do this. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. Keeping ledgers straight for 41 years turns out to be surprisingly useful for the remembering. The listening came with no training at all.

I will not pretend that every week is easy. Some are hard. When they are, the staff look after us. That matters, and it is only fair to mention it. But difficult afternoons are not the whole story of the day unit, or even most of it.

At present there are four of us on a rota designed for six. We have been two short since the summer: one volunteer moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren, and another had a knee operation. We could do with two more people joining us.

The commitment is **one Thursday a fortnight, from 1.30pm to 4pm**. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, does the induction herself. It takes about two hours. There is also a short food hygiene course online, which the hospice pays for. You are not simply handed a trolley and wished good luck.

If you are wondering whether it might suit you, come along to the **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits, and no obligation. You can ask Bridget questions, find out what is involved, and then make up your own mind. Alternatively, ring Bridget on the volunteering line.

I did not become a volunteer because I am especially good or brave. I did it because I needed somewhere to be on a Thursday, and I have kept doing it because I enjoy the company.

We need two more people. If one of them might be you, do come to the open afternoon. At the very least, there will be biscuits – although I make no promises about the bourbons.
